newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson wins full custody of his children.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson wins full custody of his children.

text.p: O.J. Simpson was awarded full custody of his two youngest children on Friday, more than 2-1/2 years after their mother was killed and their football star father was charged with her murder.
Orange County Judge Nancy Wieben Stock ruled that Sydney, 11, and Justin, 8, who have lived with their maternal grandparents since just after their mother's death, must be returned to their father.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman, issued a statement saying, "We are all so very grateful to have the children home again where they want to be."

But Natasha Roit, the Browns' attorney, denounced the judge's decision, saying living with Simpson would expose the children to "substantial risk" from a man who had beaten their mother and "has continued to deny that he is a batterer."

Louis and Judith Brown, who were granted visitation rights, said they received the news with "great sadness and concern," and their daughter Denise said her parents would appeal the ruling. "I think what happened here was devastating," a tearful Denise Brown said on CNN's "Larry King Live."

The judge's ruling capped a bitter custody fight between the Browns and Simpson, but the Hall of Fame running back's legal troubles are far from over -- he is still on trial in civil court, facing a wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.
During the custody battle, the Browns' attorneys contended Simpson was an unfit parent, citing allegations of domestic violence.

But Simpson's attorneys argued he had the right to full custody as the biological father. Simpson had also expressed concern that living with the Browns, who are white, the children were not being instructed in their black heritage.

While stating her belief that Simpson had physically abused Nicole Brown Simpson at least four times in the 1980s, the judge said the children showed no signs of "fear or intimidation" around him and there was no reason to think he would ever harm them.
But Roit suggested that one or both of the children was, in fact, fearful of Simpson.

Simpson signed temporary guardianship of the children over to the Browns after his arrest on June 17, 1994, and the children have lived with them for the past 2-1/2 years in the Orange County coastal community of Dana Point.
After his release last year, Simpson, who had weekend visits with his children, asked to get them back. The Browns refused and sought legal custody.

Under the judge's 11-page ruling, Roit said, the children can spend the upcoming holidays with Simpson, but they cannot be moved permanently out of the Browns' home before Jan. 10. Stock scheduled a hearing then on the Browns' request to stay the children's departure pending an appeal.

The children's whereabouts were not immediately known Friday night, and it was unclear exactly when they would join their father. Simpson begged "the media and the public to allow my children their privacy and to live in as normal an environment as possible."

But the Browns left no doubt about their concern for the children's safety, saying they had fought to prevent them from being exposed "to the risks and detriment of domestic violence which plagued their past and, if returned to Mr. Simpson, would be likely to affect their future."
Testifying last month at his civil trial, Simpson flatly denied ever having abused his former wife, even when a photo of her bruised, swollen face was shown to the jury.

The judge's ruling left open the possibility that the civil court jury could find Simpson responsible -- and financially liable -- for the murder of his former wife but he would still have the right to raise the children from their marriage.
Legal experts said California law favoured Simpson as the natural parent, and even the attorney appointed to represent the children recommended they be turned over to him.

The Browns' attorneys contended Simpson was a neglectful parent even before his former wife's death, preferring to spend time on the golf course with his friends rather than on the playground with his children.

But Simpson allayed the judge's concern that the children would be mostly left with a nanny by promising that his sister Shirley Baker would stay in his mansion and care for them whenever he is away, the New York Daily News reported earlier this month.
